catalog_quote: Stress and high pitch always go together and are phonemic, as shown in the following examples. 8) a. /boko'líf/ [boko'Ríp] ‘say.2/3PL’ b. /’bókolif/ [‘bókoRif] ‘be.FUT.2/3PL’ 9) a. /’kókmen/ [‘kókmen] ‘big-head’ b. /kok'mén/ [kok'mén] ‘close by’ 10) a. /’síNam/ [‘síNåm] ‘flying fox’ b. /si'Nám/ [si'Nåm] ‘far away’ Although a single word in isolation most of the times has an audible phonemic stress on one of its syllables this word within an utterance might change the stress to a different syllable or even lose it in favor of a semantically more important word in the context. Within an utterance it is rather a phrase (whether noun or verb phrase) carrying a stress than single words. ... If the single word is said in isolation, there would be stress on each of the words: 'yemen, 'taro' and i'blof, 'heart'. Within an utterance though, there are far less stresses than words. ... There is a very limited number of words which do have a contrastive tone - or rather high pitch. The semantic load of those few words is very low and the context clarifies without effort the intended meaning. ... 16) a. /fián/ [fiå@n] ‘flea’ b. /fian/ [fiån] ‘big’ 17) a. /’áluue/ [‘å@luwe] ‘hold tied’ b. /a'lúue/ [å'lúwe] ‘bark’

sweep_summary: Bimin (bimi1240) is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title are Glottolog misattachments: Villarejo et al. 2012 (GSR stress sensor, Sensors, doi:10.3390/s120506075) and Yamakoshi et al. 2008 (driver stress detection, IEEE EMBS, doi:10.1109/iembs.2008.4649346) are biomedical-engineering papers on physiological stress, irrelevant, priority none. The real stress statement for Bimin is already held by the project from our earlier reading: Weber & Whitney 1999 Bimin Phonology Essentials, sec. 4 p. 5 (p. 8), which states that stress and high pitch always co-occur and are phonemic, gives four minimal pairs distinguished by stress position, and notes phrasal re-stressing within utterances; reading = lexically contrastive (unpredictable) stress fused with high pitch. Weber 1997 Grammar Essentials adds only that clitics are unstressed (p. 16); Healey 1964 gives family-level 'all Mountain-Ok languages appear to have contrastive lexical pitch' (p. 61) with no Bimin examples. Weber 2003 Bimin OPD (6 pp.) remains unobtainable (SIL 403 on both hosts, no archived copy at the Internet Archive), priority medium since it could only refine the 1999 statement. Crossref DOI lookups and SIL/the Internet Archive retries were done by automated download. Record appended to

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (14 pp., text; title page 'Bimin Phonology Essentials, Bimin Language (Bim Weng / Nimtew Weng), Ethnologue Code: bhl, Thomas Weber & Henry Whitney, SIL PNG, March 1999'). Section 4 'PITCH/STRESS/ACCENT' is on printed p. 5 = p. 8, continuing to p. 6, exactly as the locator says. The prose of the quote is there verbatim: 'Stress and high pitch always go together and are phonemic, as shown in the following examples.'.. 'Although a single word in isolation most of the times has an audible phonemic stress on one of its syllables this word within an utterance might change the stress to a different syllable or even lose it in favor of a semantically more important word in the context…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (realised together with high pitch) is phonemic/lexically contrastive: its position is not predictable and distinguishes minimal pairs (initial vs final stress in di- and trisyllables); the transcribed word list shows stress on initial, medial or final syllables item by item. No default position rule is given. The authors add that only a small number of words actually contrast by pitch/stress and the functional load is low.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described; 'minor stress' is mentioned only at utterance level (e.g. a minor stress on the first syllable of a non-focal word in a sentence).
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics have no stress of their own and lean on the preceding word (Grammar Essentials 1997 p. 17); the clitics sako/tako/tewe have a more stressed first syllable. Contrastive high pitch limited to 'a very limited number of words' with low semantic load.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word in isolation (citation form): 'a single word in isolation most of the times has an audible phonemic stress on one of its syllables'; in connected speech stress is assigned per phrase, may move to another syllable or be lost depending on information structure/speaker intention. Stress and high pitch are treated as a single prosodic prominence (pitch accent-like).
new_statements.identity_note: Weber & Whitney 1999 describe Bimin = 'Bim Weng' (main valley, SE Sandaun Province; Bim and Kuskis phratries) with notes on the southern 'Nimtew Weng' dialect (Western Province; Kasan and Kuel phratries); both are the language-level unit bimi1240 (ISO bhl); data mainly from Bim Weng speakers (Akalu village area). Healey 1964's 'Bimin' (Wonggop valley clans Bimin, Kuskusmin, Kwelmin, Kasanmin) is the same language but he gives no Bimin-specific prosodic statement.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Weber & Whitney 1999: stress and high pitch go together and are phonemic, minimal pairs by position). The 2003 OPD repeats two of the same pairs (bókolif/bokolíf, kókmen/kokmén) but describes the contrast as 'contrastive tone or pitch' and restricts it to 'a very limited number of words'; it does not call it stress in the prose and states no default stress position. So it supports the catalog's lexical/pitch accent-like classification while adding that the lexical contrast is marginal in the vocabulary; it does not supply a fixed-position rule that would contradict the record. Variety: Akaru dialect (running header).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The OPD gives no positional stress rule. Under 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' it says only that a very limited number of words carry a contrastive tone or pitch, illustrated by pairs that differ solely in which syllable bears the (acute-marked) high pitch: bókolif 'they are' vs bokolíf 'they talk', kókmen 'stop that!' vs kokmén 'close to'. These are the same minimal pairs Weber & Whitney 1999 give for 'phonemic stress fused with high pitch'; the 2003 sheet labels the contrast tone/pitch and stresses that it is confined to few words. Nothing else in the 6 pages (inventory, vowel sequences, syllable patterns, phonological conventions, text) bears on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the contrast is said to hold for 'a very limited number of words' only; no default placement is stated for the rest of the lexicon
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Bimin [Bimin Weng], ISO bhl, Akaru dialect (running header 'Bimin [Akaru dialect] OPD'), Sandaun / Western Province, Mountain Ok; population 2,000-2,500 (2001); data checked by Thomas Weber, April 2003; predecessor Weber & Weber 1992 OPD cited in its bibliography.

sources.note: Sec. 4 'Pitch/stress/accent' (p. 5): stress and high pitch always co-occur and are phonemic; minimal pairs by stress position ('bókolif vs boko'líf, 'kókmen vs kok'mén, 'síNam vs si'Nám, 'áluue vs a'lúue); a word in isolation usually has one audible phonemic stress, but in utterances stress is phrase-level and may shift or disappear; only a very limited number of words carry contrastive high pitch, low functional load. Word list in sec. 3.3 marks stress on varying syllables (initial, medial, final).
